intro: Rachmaninoff records his C♯ minor Prelude in New York in April 1928, thirty-six years after writing it. The quiet chords at the start return as a whole keyboard of bells.

sections.label: A · Bells, then rushing triplets
sections.mNote: Three low notes introduce the Lento

sections.label: B · Triplets gather force
sections.mNote: The Agitato melody rises above the running notes

sections.label: C · Descending chords and returning bells
sections.mNote: The rush leads back to the opening chords

sections.label: D · Quiet chords over C♯
sections.mNote: A held bass supports the last slow chords

cues.title: Bells and a whisper
cues.text: Three low notes, A–G♯–C♯, sound in octaves. Rachmaninoff marks them fortissimo, then drops to ppp for the chordal answer. The piano has scarcely begun before it falls to a whisper.
cues.evidence: Bosworth (1896) and Universal Edition (1910), opening upbeat and bars 1–4; Petro Kostandy’s Mutopia engraving. https://www.mutopiaproject.org/cgibin/piece-info.cgi?id=2033
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: The right hand divides
cues.text: In the Agitato, the right hand carries a descending E–D♯–D♮–C♯ melody while triplets turn beneath it. The left hand reaches down for bass notes, then rises to answer the tune.
cues.evidence: Bosworth and Universal Edition score, bars 14–21: separately stemmed upper melody, triplet quavers and the answering left-hand line. https://www.mutopiaproject.org/cgibin/piece-info.cgi?id=2033
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: Two days in the studio
cues.text: On 21 March 1928, Rachmaninoff makes three takes of the Prelude in Camden, New Jersey. Victor discards all three. On 4 April he tries again in New York; the second take that day becomes the published record.
cues.evidence: Discography of American Historical Recordings, Victor matrix BVE-25650: takes 19–21 marked Destroy; takes 22–23 dated 4 April 1928, with take 23 the master. https://adp.library.ucsb.edu/index.php/matrix/detail/700010910/BVE-25650-Prelude_in_C_sharp_minor

cues.title: The piano fills four staves
cues.text: Tempo primo: the opening returns, vastly enlarged. The score spreads the piano over four staves and marks the chords fff pesante. The bass keeps tolling while both hands strike the tune in octaves.
cues.evidence: Bosworth and Universal Edition score, bars 45–48: four-stave notation, Tempo primo and fff pesante. https://www.mutopiaproject.org/cgibin/piece-info.cgi?id=2033
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: The bass stays on C♯
cues.text: The closing chords settle over a low C♯ held across the bars. After so many repeated blows, the last chord simply stays: C♯ minor, ppp, with a fermata above it.
cues.evidence: Bosworth and Universal Edition score, bars 55–61: C♯ pedal and final ppp chord with fermata. https://www.mutopiaproject.org/cgibin/piece-info.cgi?id=2033
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

composer.epithet: In exile he earned his living at the piano, while the bells of his Russian childhood kept sounding through the music he wrote.
facts: Zverev and Siloti at the piano; Taneyev and Arensky in composition
Ivanovka, Dresden, New York, Villa Senar and Beverly Hills
Four piano concertos, three symphonies, three completed operas, choral music, songs and piano works

quote.text: I feel like a ghost wandering in a world grown alien. I cannot cast out the old way of writing, and I cannot acquire the new.
quote.source: Rachmaninoff to Leonard Liebling, 1939; published in The Musical Courier, 5 April 1943

composer.background:
“My hearty thanks to the old man for not having forgotten about me!” Rachmaninoff wrote to the singer Mikhail Slonov on 26 December 1892. The old man was Tchaikovsky, who had praised his opera Aleko in a newspaper interview. Rachmaninoff was nineteen, newly graduated from the Moscow Conservatory with its Great Gold Medal. Tchaikovsky helped get the opera into the Bolshoi, and in May 1893 sat in the audience applauding. For a young composer, it was an excellent beginning.

His childhood had been less orderly. Born into a landowning family, he grew up at Oneg, near Novgorod, until his father’s financial failures forced a move to St Petersburg. He entered the Conservatory there in 1883. His parents separated; his sister Sofia died of diphtheria; schoolwork went badly. His grandmother took him to Orthodox services, where he heard the voices and bells that would stay with him. In 1885 his cousin Alexander Siloti recommended a move to Moscow, under the formidable care of the piano teacher Nikolai Zverev.
